name: The Hebrew Bible
fw: CCSS RL/RI/RH / C3 / IL SS 9–12 / Teaching About Religion
fwnote: The course reads a tradition's texts as literature and as historical sources in a public school, so it cites the reading standards for the band (RL, RI, RH, WHST), C3 history for 6–8, Illinois SS.H 9–12, and one of the six principles in "A Teacher's Guide to Religion in the Public Schools" (First Amendment Center) that the AAR 2010 Guidelines build on; alignment is the course author's judgment, not a certification or an endorsement by any of these bodies.

1.bq: What do the first stories in the Torah say about the world, rest and promises?
std: RL.K.2
With prompting and support, retell familiar stories with their key details.
Retell stories with key details and show you understand their central message or lesson.
Compare two versions of the same story told by different authors or from different cultures.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
1.write: Pick one story from this unit: the first week (Genesis 1–2) or Noah (Genesis 6–9). Draw or write what the Torah says happened. Then tell one thing Jewish families do to remember it, like Shabbat candles or the rainbow blessing.
rooms: Daily Practice — The Bible, grades K–2

ch.t: Seven Days and Shabbat
ch.bq: What does the first story in the Torah say happened in the very first week?
ch.talk: Why do you think Maya's family lights candles before they tell the story of the first week?

s.t: The Torah and Its First Book

l.look: How many books are in the Torah? Hold up that many fingers.
What two big things does this first line say were made?
Close your eyes. Now open them. What do you see because of light?
Which light do you see right now? Is it day or night?
Add up the days. How many days of making are there?
What did God do on the seventh day, in the story?
What is on a Shabbat table? Count the things in the list.
If you had a garden to care for, what would you do first?

ch.t: Noah, the Ark and the Rainbow
ch.bq: What does the Torah say a promise is, and how did Noah's family learn about one?
ch.talk: Why did everyone cheer when they saw the leaf? What did the leaf tell them?

l.look: Which number is the biggest? Was the ark longer or taller?
Pick an animal. Say its name two times, one for each in the pair.
Which number is the biggest? Which is the smallest?
How did the leaf tell Noah the water was going down?
What is the rainbow a sign of, in the story?
What happens to a big job when people cannot understand each other?
How many traditions in this lesson tell a story of Noah?

2.bq: What do the Torah's stories of Abraham's family say about promises, kindness and forgiving?
std: Describe the characters, settings and major events of a story using key details.
Retell stories, fables and folktales from different cultures and state the lesson or message they teach.
Teaching About Religion · aware not accepting
Build students' understanding of religions without pressing them to accept any one.
2.write: Pick one person from this unit: Abraham (Genesis 18), Rebekah (Genesis 24), Jacob (Genesis 28) or Joseph (Genesis 45). Draw or write one kind or brave thing the Torah says they did. Then tell what Jewish tradition says we can learn from it.
rooms: Daily Practice — The Bible, grades K–2

ch.t: Abraham and Sarah Go to a New Land
ch.bq: What does the Torah say Abraham and Sarah did when they left home, and how did they treat people?
ch.talk: Abraham ran to help strangers on a hot day. What do you do when a guest comes to your home?
ch.story: Three Travelers in the Hot Sun

l.look: "Get thee out" is an old way to say "go." What three things does the story say Abram had to leave?

l.t: A Promise of a Big Family
l.look: Why do you think the story uses stars to talk about a big family?
Abraham ran. He did not walk. What does that tell you about how he felt about guests?
Why would a tent with four doors be good for guests? What is one way our classroom could be like that tent?
Which number is the biggest? Why do you think Sarah laughed?
Rebekah did not have to water the camels. Why do you think she did it?
Isaac and Rebekah had two sons. Who do you think they were? The next chapter will tell you.

ch.t: Jacob, Rachel, Leah and Joseph
ch.bq: What does the Torah say happened to Jacob's family, and how did the twelve tribes get their names?
ch.talk: Jacob was alone and far from home. How do you think the dream made him feel?

l.look: The Torah says the twins were very different. What is one way you are different from someone in your family?
"Ascending" means going up. "Descending" means going down. Show with your hand what the angels were doing.
The Torah says seven years felt like a few days to Jacob because he loved Rachel. What makes time feel fast for you?
Jacob got a new name after he held on all night. What is something hard you kept trying at?
How many sons did Jacob have? How many tribes? What do you notice?
What do you think the brothers thought the dream meant? How would you feel if you were a brother?
Joseph told Pharaoh to save food in the good years. Why was that a smart plan?
Joseph chose to forgive. What is one kind thing you could say to someone who was mean to you?

3.bq: What does the Torah say about leaving Egypt and the mountain, and how do Jewish families remember it every year?
std: Retell stories with key details and show you understand their central message or lesson.
Ask and answer who, what, where, when, why and how questions about a story's key details.
Teaching About Religion · study not practice
Teach about religious practices without having students take part in them.
3.write: Draw or tell the story of one night: the night the people left Egypt, or the day at the mountain. Use the Torah's words from Exodus 12 (the flat bread) or Exodus 20 (the ten sayings). Say what the Torah says happened, and say one thing a Jewish family does today to remember it.
rooms: Daily Practice — The Bible, grades K–2

ch.t: Out of Egypt: The Passover Story
ch.bq: What does the Torah say happened when the people left Egypt, and why do Jewish families tell it every year?
ch.talk: Why do you think the youngest child gets to ask the big question at the Passover table?

l.look: Which book of the Torah comes before Exodus? Say its name.
What do you think the girl behind the reeds is feeling? What is she waiting for?

l.t: A Bush That Did Not Burn Up
l.look: "Consumed" means burned up. What was strange about this fire?
Who is talking to Pharaoh here, and who is the message from?

l.t: Bread With No Time to Rise
l.look: Which bread would you take if you had to leave right now? Why does the Passover table have that one?
Miriam sings this with a drum. What just happened that made her want to sing?
How many questions does the youngest child ask? Try asking one.

ch.t: Mount Sinai and the Ten Sayings
ch.bq: What does the Torah say the people heard at the mountain, and how do Jewish families keep those words today?
ch.talk: Which rule would you write for your room? Why would it make the room a better place?

l.look: Which number is on this list two times? Point to it.
How do you think the people at the bottom feel? What would you do if you were there?

l.t: One God and a Day of Rest
l.look: Sabbath is the English word for Shabbat. What does this saying ask people to do?

l.t: Family, Truth and What Is Yours
l.look: "Thy" is an old word for "your." What is one way to honor a parent this week?
Which number is the biggest? Is 613 more or less than 10?
Which table comes first in the year? Which part of the story comes first?

l.t: The Torah Scroll in the Synagogue
l.look: Why do you think people stand up when the scroll is carried?

4.bq: What is the Tanakh, and what one story do its first five books tell?
std: Use text features and search tools, such as key words and labels, to locate information quickly.
Determine the main idea of a text, explain how details support it, and summarize.
Teaching About Religion · expose not impose
Introduce a range of religious views without imposing any particular one.
4.write: Is the Torah one story or five separate books? Use Genesis 12:1–5 (Abram leaves home), Exodus 20:8 (one of the Ten Sayings) and Deuteronomy 34:1–5 (Moses on Mount Nebo). Say what each passage says, and explain how Jewish tradition connects them with the idea of covenant.

ch.t: Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim
ch.bq: What is the Tanakh, and how do Jewish communities read it?
ch.talk: Why do you think Jewish communities read the scroll one piece at a time, instead of all at once?
ch.story: A Scroll That Takes a Year

l.look: Make up a three-part name for something you know, using its first letters, and explain what each letter stands for.
Add the first three rows. Do they match the last row? Which part has the most books?
Put each of the six books in its part, and say one clue that helped you.
Which alphabet has the fewest letters? How many more letters does English have than Hebrew?
Write your own name and one short sentence without vowels. Trade with a partner. Was it easy or hard to read?
Ezra was called a scribe. What two jobs does this passage show a scribe doing?
This line is written inside the Torah scroll and is also said in Jewish prayer. Why might a community keep a sentence in a scroll and also say it every day?
There are 54 portions but only 52 weeks. What must happen in some weeks?
Why might a community celebrate the end of a book by starting it again instead of putting it away?
In Hebrew this verse begins with the word Bereshit. Which English words in the translation match that one Hebrew word?

ch.t: The Torah's Big Story
ch.bq: What one long story do the five books of the Torah tell, from the first day to the edge of the land?
ch.talk: If you had to pick one footprint as the most important stop in the story, which would it be, and why?

l.t: The Hebrew Names of the Books
l.look: Which book is the longest? Add up all five. About how many chapters is the whole Torah?
What is Abram asked to leave behind, and what is he promised? Which would be harder for you: leaving or trusting the promise?

l.t: Shemot: Slaves and a Baby in a Basket
l.look: What does each woman risk? Why do you think the Torah tells us about them before it tells us about Moses's big deeds?

l.t: The Night of Passover and the Sea
l.look: Which of these numbers does a Jewish family act out at home every spring? How?
This is one of the Ten Sayings. Which day does it point to, and how did you see Jewish families keep it in the last chapter?
The rule about loving a neighbor comes right after a rule about grudges. Why might the Torah put those two ideas together?
Why might people who saw the same thing give such different reports? Which report would you have believed, and why?

s.t: Last Words and a New Leader

l.look: Moses is speaking to people who will live in the land without him. Why do you think he ends with a choice instead of an order?
Moses leads the people for forty years and then sees the land only from far away. How do you think a reader should feel at this ending? What might Jewish tradition find hopeful in it?
Put the seven stops in the order the Torah tells them, and name the book where each one happens.

5.bq: What do the books of Joshua, Judges, Ruth and 1 Samuel say about courage, loyalty and the kind of leader a people needs?
std: Describe a character's traits, motives and feelings and how the character's actions move the events.
Work out a story's theme from its details and summarize the text.
Teaching About Religion · educate not promote or denigrate
Present every tradition fairly, neither advancing nor disparaging religion.
5.write: What kind of leader do these books say a people needs? Pick two people from the unit, like Deborah (Judges 4), Gideon (Judges 7), Ruth (Ruth 1) or Samuel (1 Samuel 3 or 8). For each, tell what the text says they did and what Jewish readers have seen in it. Then say what the two stories have in common.

ch.t: Joshua, Deborah, Gideon, Samson
ch.bq: What do the books of Joshua and Judges say about courage, trust and choices?
ch.talk: Why do you think people walked so far to ask Deborah what was right? What makes a person someone others trust?
ch.story: The Judge Under the Palm Tree

l.look: The old words "thee" and "thou" mean "you." What is Joshua told to do? What reason is he given?
How many times did the people walk around Jericho in all? Add the six days and the seventh day.
Why might it help to have the Levites, who led worship, living in every part of the land instead of in one place?
Which book is shortest? Which two books together have more chapters than 1 Samuel?
Find two jobs the text gives Deborah. Where did people go to see her?
The text gives a reason the army had to be small. What was it? Look at how much smaller 300 is than 32,000.
What kind of strength does each one have? Which kind do you think the book wants readers to notice?
Samson had already lied to Delilah three times. Why do you think he told the truth this time? What does the story say about trust?
Is this line a wish, a warning, or both? What in the book makes you think so?
By Ben Zoma's measure, was Samson strong? Was Deborah? Explain using one story from this chapter.

ch.t: Ruth, Hannah and Samuel
ch.bq: How do the stories of Ruth, Hannah and Samuel show loyalty and kindness, and how did Israel come to ask for a king?
ch.talk: Ruth could have gone home like Orpah. Why do you think she stayed with Naomi instead? What did it cost her?
ch.story: A Promise on a Dusty Road

l.look: Why does Naomi want a new name? What has changed for her? What has she not lost?

l.t: Where You Go, I Will Go
l.look: "Entreat" means beg. "Whither" means where. Count how many things Ruth promises in this one verse.
Ruth was both poor and a stranger. How does this law from the Torah help explain what she does in Boaz's field?
Why might the book end with this family list? What does it say about who can belong to the people of Israel?
Seven weeks is forty-nine days. What number day is Shavuot? Why might a harvest holiday be a good day to read a story about a field?
The rabbis turned a story into rules. Find each rule and the part of Hannah's story it comes from.
"Heareth" means hears. Who taught Samuel to answer this way? Why might it matter that he says he is listening, not talking?
Why might a judge travel to different towns instead of staying in one place? Think about who could reach him.

s.t: The People Ask for a King

l.look: The people heard this warning and still wanted a king. Why do you think they did? Was Samuel right to warn them?
Pick one person from this chapter. Which of the three things in this saying did they do? Give one example from the text.

6.bq: What do the books of Samuel, Kings and the Prophets say about power, fairness and turning back?
std: Describe a character's traits, motives and feelings and how the character's actions move the events.
Determine a theme from how characters respond to challenges, and summarize the text.
Teaching About Religion · inform not conform
Inform students about beliefs without asking them to conform to any.
6.write: What does the Tanakh say a leader should be? Pick two or three passages from this unit, such as 1 Samuel 8:11-18, 1 Samuel 16:7, 2 Samuel 12:1-7, 1 Kings 3:5-12 or Amos 5:21-24. Say what each passage says and how Jewish tradition or another reader has read it. Then give your own answer to the question, using the text.

ch.t: Saul, David and Solomon
ch.bq: What do the books of Samuel and Kings say a good king should be, and what happens when kings fall short?
ch.talk: Why do you think the story introduces David with a harp before it shows him with a sword?
ch.story: A Harp for a Troubled King

l.look: What is the biggest cost Samuel says a king will bring? Why do you think the people said yes anyway?
Why might a tall, strong man hide on the day he is made king? What does this tell you about Saul?
"Outward appearance" means what a person looks like. What does this verse say matters more? How does it fit the choice of David?
David picked up five stones but used one. Why do you think the story tells us he took five?
What does it mean for a friendship to "not depend on a thing"? Why did the rabbis pick David and Jonathan as the example?
Why might a king choose a capital city that belongs to no single tribe? Can you think of a modern example?

l.t: Nathan and the Poor Man's Lamb
l.look: Why did Nathan tell a story about a lamb instead of just saying what David did? What did the story make David do?

l.t: David in the Psalms and in Prayer
l.look: "I shall not want" means I will not lack what I need. Why might a former shepherd picture God as a shepherd?
The king never planned to hurt the baby. What was he really testing? What did each woman's answer show?
A cubit is about a foot and a half. About how long was the Temple in feet? Was it bigger or smaller than your school gym?
How many years did the northern kingdom last after the split? How many years did Judah last?

ch.t: Elijah, Jonah and the Prophets of Justice
ch.bq: What is a prophet in the Tanakh, and why do prophets so often say what people do not want to hear?
ch.talk: Jonah runs away from a message. Why might Jewish tradition choose to read this story on the day for saying sorry?
ch.story: A Boat Going the Wrong Way

l.t: A Messenger, Not a Fortune Teller
l.look: In your own words, what is the difference between a fortune teller and a messenger? Which one is a navi?
Why do you think the story says Elijah soaked his own altar with water before he prayed?
The wind, the earthquake and the fire were loud and big. Why might the text put the voice after all of them, and make it small?
Why do you think families set a cup for a prophet from long ago? What does an open door say to a guest?

l.t: Amos: Be Fair to the Poor
l.look: Water in a stream keeps moving and reaches everyone downstream. Why is that a good picture for justice?
A plowshare grows food and a sword hurts people. What is Isaiah saying the nations will do with their weapons?
The text gives Nineveh forty days. Where else in the Tanakh have you seen the number forty? What might it mean here?
Why do you think the book ends with a question and no answer? What would you say back if you were Jonah?
Imagine you are choosing one story to read on the day for saying sorry. Why would Jonah be a good choice? Why might it be a hard choice?

s.t: Jeremiah and the Fall of Jerusalem

l.look: Have you ever had something you felt you had to say? How does Jeremiah describe what it feels like to hold a message in?
Put these events in order on a line. How many years passed between the burning of Jerusalem and the return?

7.bq: How do the songs, sayings and scrolls of the Ketuvim give people words for joy, sorrow, courage and hope?
std: Explain how poems, drama and prose differ, using their structural elements.
Work out a story's theme from its details and summarize the text.
Teaching About Religion · study not practice
Teach about religious practices without having students take part in them.
7.write: The Ketuvim give people words for hard times and happy times. Pick one feeling: joy, sorrow, courage or hope. Find two or three passages from this unit that speak to it (for example Psalm 23:1, Proverbs 15:1, Job 1:21, Esther 4:14, Lamentations 1:1, Ecclesiastes 3:1 or Nehemiah 8:8). Explain what each passage says and how Jewish readers use it during the year.

ch.t: Psalms and Proverbs
ch.bq: How do the songs and sayings in the Ketuvim put big feelings and big questions into words?
ch.talk: Why do you think one short song can fit a quiet hospital room and a loud stadium at the same time?

l.look: Which psalm is the longest? Which is the shortest? How many times longer is the longest one than Psalm 23?
"I shall not want" means "I will not be missing anything I need." Why would a sheep with a good shepherd feel that way?
Psalm 150 lists horns, harps, drums, flutes and cymbals. Why do you think the book of Psalms ends with such a loud song?
In each verse, what is the one idea the two lines share? Try writing your own two-line echo about your favorite place.
Which psalm is said on Shabbat? Which two days have psalm numbers that are next to each other?
Think of a time someone was angry with you. What would a "soft answer" sound like? What would a "grievous word" sound like?

l.t: Wisdom Is a Tree of Life
l.look: "Her" means wisdom. If wisdom is a road, what would walking on it look like in a classroom?

s.t: Hard Questions and a Love Song

l.look: Job says these words right after he loses everything. What do they show about how he feels at first? How might a person feel later?
Why might a book answer a hard question with more questions? Do you think Job got what he wanted? Explain.
List the signs of spring in these lines. Why would a spring poem fit a spring holiday like Passover?

ch.t: Esther, Daniel and Going Home
ch.bq: How do the last books of the Ketuvim tell about speaking up, staying strong far from home, and going home again?
ch.talk: Why do you think people make noise at Haman's name instead of just listening quietly to the story?
ch.story: Noise Every Time the Villain Is Named

l.look: Which one person's choice starts the trouble? Which one person's choice ends it? Explain.

l.t: For Such a Time as This
l.look: "Come to royal estate" means "become queen." What is Mordecai asking Esther to think about? Have you ever been in the right place at the right time to help?
Which scroll is the shortest? Which is the longest? How many chapters are in all five together?
What did Daniel want to keep from home? Why might he ask for a test instead of just refusing the food?
Daniel says he did no wrong to the king even though he broke the king's law. How can both things be true?

s.t: A Sad Poem and a Wise Poem

l.look: "Solitary" means alone. The poem pictures the city as a person. What feeling does the picture of a widow give the reader?
Chapter 3 goes on: a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance. Write two pairs of your own, like "a time to run and a time to rest."
About how many years passed between the burning of the First Temple and Cyrus's message? Remember, BCE years count down.

l.t: Nehemiah's Wall and a Big Reading
l.look: "Gave the sense" means explained the meaning. Why was explaining as important as reading? How is this like a teacher reading aloud today?

l.t: The Last Book: Let Him Go Up
l.look: Why might it matter that the last word of the whole Tanakh is about going up to Jerusalem, not about a disaster?

8.bq: How did the Tanakh get its shape and its text, and how does Jewish tradition read it?
std: Analyze how events and developments connect within their wider historical setting.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases in a text, including terms specific to history and society.
Describe how a text presents information, such as in order, by comparison or by cause.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
8.write: Does Jewish tradition treat the text of the Tanakh as fixed or as open? Argue your answer using at least two of these: the scribe's rules and the Masoretes' counting (chapter 15), the story of the oven with Deuteronomy 30:12 (Bava Metzia 59b), Rashi on Genesis 1:1, and the midrash on Abraham and the idols (Genesis Rabbah 38:13). Explain what each shows and how Jewish readers have understood it.
rooms: How to read a sacred text — the room

ch.t: Three Parts, Twenty-Four Books, One Scroll
ch.bq: How did the Tanakh get its shape, and how has its text been kept the same for so long?
ch.talk: Why might a community decide that a scroll with one wrong letter cannot be used? What would be lost if scribes were less careful?

l.look: The Prophets part has eight books but takes up many pages. Which of its books do you think hold more than one short book inside?
Compare this ending with the last verse of Malachi in a Christian Bible, which warns of a coming day of judgment. What feeling does each ending leave with a reader?
Song of Songs is a love poem that never names God. Why might some rabbis have questioned it, and why might Rabbi Akiva have defended it so strongly?
The Hebrew verse has only seven words. Count the English words. What does a translator have to add to make Hebrew sound like English?
Why might the translator change "went down" to "revealed himself"? What does that choice tell you about what his listeners believed about God?
How many centuries passed between the oldest known biblical text and the vowel system used today? What kept the reading steady in between?
How could counting the middle verse, word and letter help that scribe know his copy was complete? What are the limits of that method?
About how many years separate the Great Isaiah Scroll from the Aleppo Codex? Why does it matter that the two texts of Isaiah are so alike?

l.t: How a Torah Scroll Is Made
l.look: If a scribe writes about 1,000 letters a day, roughly how many days of writing does one scroll take? What else might slow the work down?
How would a member of the congregation explain what they are doing and why? What does the practice say about how the community sees the words in the scroll?
The verse says the readers "gave the sense." How could a melody that shows where phrases break help a listener understand a text?

ch.t: How Jews Read: Parashah, Midrash, Commentary
ch.bq: How does Jewish tradition read the Tanakh, and why does it treat arguing about a verse as a way of honoring it?
ch.talk: Why might a community keep printing old disagreements beside a verse instead of printing just one correct explanation?

l.look: A year has 52 weeks, and some of them are holidays. How does a community fit 54 portions into one year?
What word or image links the two passages? Why might the people who chose this haftarah want listeners to hear the flood story and Isaiah's promise on the same morning?
Why might a tradition require ten people before a scroll may be read? What does a minimum number say about the kind of reading it is?
The midrash takes a fact about a letter's shape and turns it into a lesson. What is the rabbi actually teaching about how to read? Do you find the method convincing?
List what the Torah leaves out here. Which of those gaps does the midrash about the idols fill, and what does it leave alone?
What are the limits of this idea? If a verse can mean many things, how would a rabbi decide that a reading is wrong?
Give one peshat reading: who is the man, in the story as told? Then give one derash reading: what else could the night fight stand for? Which question is each reading answering?
Why might a tradition that prizes deep study also tell a story in which deep study harms three out of four? What kind of reader does the story praise?
What does this comment assume about the purpose of the Torah? How does Rashi turn a question about order into a claim about meaning?
How many years separate the earliest and the latest commentator on the page? What does it mean to print them as if they were in one room?
In Deuteronomy the verse says the commandment is close and doable. Rabbi Joshua uses it to say a heavenly voice cannot decide a legal debate. Is that a peshat reading or a derash reading? Explain.

9.bq: How do Genesis and Exodus turn the story of a world, a family and a rescue into the covenant that the rest of the Tanakh builds on?
std: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of primary and secondary sources.
Identify parts of a text that reveal an author's point of view or purpose.
Determine a theme, analyze how it develops through characters, setting and plot, and summarize objectively.
Teaching About Religion · aware not accepting
Build students' understanding of religions without pressing them to accept any one.
9.write: Does the Torah want its readers to remember slavery or to forget it? Argue from the text. Cite at least two of these: Exodus 20:2, Exodus 22:20 (JPS numbering) or 23:9, Deuteronomy 5:15, Exodus 13:8. Explain what each passage says and how at least one reader (Rashi, the Mishnah, the Haggadah, or the singers of "Go Down, Moses") has read it.

ch.t: Genesis: From Creation to Joseph
ch.bq: How does the book of Genesis tie a creation story, a flood, and one family's promises into a single thread?
ch.talk: Genesis 22 never says what Isaac was thinking. Why might a storyteller leave that out on purpose, and what does the reader have to do because of it?

l.t: Two Ways to Tell a Beginning
l.look: Read the verses slowly. What already exists before God speaks? What is the first thing made by speech alone?

l.t: The Garden and the First Brothers
l.look: Both readings start from the same words in Genesis 3. Name one detail in the story that each reader might point to for support.
Pick two items the stories share and one item where Genesis clearly goes its own way. What does the difference show about what the Torah cares about?

l.t: Babel and the Shape of Genesis
l.look: Most of the book is about one family. What does that tell you about what the writers of Genesis most wanted to say?
Count the things Abram is told to leave and the things he is promised. Which list is longer? Why might the storyteller build it that way?
The text says Hagar's eyes were opened to a well. Was the well new, or had she not seen it? What might Rashi's comment add to how a reader understands the scene?
Rashi hears four steps in this one verse: thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, Isaac. What changes for a reader who hears it as a slow conversation rather than a single blunt order?
The narrator never says Jacob did wrong. Do you think the second scene is the text's way of judging the first? What clues support your view?

l.t: Leah, Rachel and a Night of Wrestling
l.look: Each reading changes what the new name Israel means. Pick one reading and explain what "he strives with God" would mean under it.

l.t: Joseph: A Story With a Shape
l.look: Joseph gives his own reading of the pit, the prison and the palace. Does the narrator ever say this directly, or only Joseph? Why might that matter?

l.t: What Archaeology Can and Cannot Say
l.look: The Gilgamesh copy is older than any copy of Genesis, but the poem itself is older still. Why can a copy's date and a story's date be so different?

ch.t: Exodus: Liberation, Sinai, the Mishkan
ch.bq: How does the book of Exodus move from slavery to freedom to law to building, and why has its story been told and sung so far beyond ancient Israel?
ch.talk: The same story of leaving Egypt is retold at a Seder table and in a spiritual sung under slavery. What does each group of singers need the story to do for them?

l.t: Slavery and a Baby in a Basket
l.look: The narrator never says these women were heroes. How does the order of the scenes make the point without saying it?
The Hebrew can also be read as "I will be what I will be." How does the meaning shift when the verb is future rather than present? Which reading fits a people about to leave slavery?

l.t: Ten Plagues and the First Passover
l.look: Which of these numbers come from the Torah itself, and which from later Jewish practice? How can you tell the two apart?
Find the two halves of the line. How does the second half give the reason for the first? Then compare Miriam's line in 15:21, which repeats it almost word for word.

Jewish tradition counts this as the first of the ten. Some Christian traditions call it an introduction. What changes about the whole list if its first item is a reminder of rescue rather than a rule?
Why does the Torah give a memory as the reason for a law, instead of just giving the law? What happens to the law when the memory fades?

l.t: The Golden Calf and the Thirteen Attributes
l.look: The passage lists mercy first and only then says the guilty are not simply cleared. Why might the tradition choose to stop its recitation before the harder words?

l.t: Why Half the Book Is a Tent
l.look: Add up the chapters about the Mishkan. What share of the book is that? If you were editing Exodus, would you keep both the instructions and the building? Why might the text repeat them?

l.t: The Haggadah: A Book That Retells a Book
l.look: The verse says "for me," even though the speaker was born long after. How does the Seder try to make that sentence feel true? Name two things done at the table that help.
When a story is borrowed, what stays the same and what changes? List one thing the singers kept exactly and one thing they changed to fit their lives.
Sort the five items into evidence for, evidence against, and evidence that cuts neither way. Which item do you find hardest to place, and why?

10.t: Torah: Leviticus to Deuteronomy, and the Former Prophets
10.bq: How do law, story and history work together in the Torah's last books and the Former Prophets to explain who Israel is and why its kingdom fell?
std: Detect gaps and limits in the historical record by comparing different kinds of sources.
Determine a source's central ideas and give an accurate summary free of prior opinions.
Analyze how a primary source and a secondary source on the same topic relate to each other.
Teaching About Religion · educate not promote or denigrate
Present every tradition fairly, neither advancing nor disparaging religion.
10.write: The book of Kings says Josiah tore his clothes when a found scroll was read to him, and then reformed worship. Using 2 Kings 22:8–13, 2 Kings 23:1–3 and one passage from Deuteronomy (such as 6:4–9 or 12:5–14), explain what the scroll seems to have demanded and how Jewish tradition and modern scholars each account for the scroll's origin.

ch.t: Holiness, the Wilderness and Moses's Last Words
ch.bq: How do the last three books of the Torah turn a rescued people into a community with a way of life?
ch.talk: The sisters did not break a rule or protest. They asked a question. Why might the text tell it this way, and what does it suggest about how laws can change?
ch.story: Five Sisters at the Tent Door

l.t: The Book That Begins With a Call
l.look: Numbers has the most chapters, but Leviticus is often called the hardest to read. Why might length and difficulty be different things?
The verse says the day cleanses the people. The rabbis added that wrongs against a neighbor must be settled with the neighbor first. How does that reading add to the verse?
The verse first says what not to do, then what to do. Why might the text put vengeance and grudges right before the command to love?

s.t: Bamidbar: Forty Years in the Wilderness

l.look: Judah is counted as the largest tribe. Which later figures in the Tanakh come from Judah, and why might the text stress its size?
What is actually different between the two reports? Why might a text make the difference a matter of trust rather than of facts?
Balaam answers the donkey as if a talking animal were normal. What might the text be saying about him by having him miss the strangeness of it?
The ruling names the sisters and then makes a rule for everyone. Why might a law that started with one family's request carry more weight than a rule with no story behind it?
The rabbis asked how love can be commanded. Rashi and later readers offered answers. What would you say it means to be told to love with all your might?

l.t: The Stranger, the Poor and the Field
l.look: The verse gives a reason for the command. How does remembering your own hard past change how a community treats newcomers?

l.t: Blessings, Curses and a Mountain Grave
l.look: Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses. What is the effect of framing a choice as something the whole world is watching?

s.t: Law as a Way of Life

l.look: The rabbis matched 365 to the days of the year and 248 to parts of the body. What might those matches be meant to say about where and when the commands apply?

l.t: A Way of Life, Read Every Year
l.look: Both readers take the verse seriously. How are their questions different, and could one reader's answer help the other?

ch.t: Joshua to Kings: The Land, the Monarchy, the Fall
ch.bq: How do the books from Joshua to Kings tell the story of a people gaining a land and a king, and losing both?
ch.talk: The scroll's words were not new; the text says they had been forgotten. What does it mean for a community to rediscover a book it already had?
ch.story: The Scroll in the Temple Wall

l.look: Samuel and Kings together are about twice the length of Joshua and Judges. What does that suggest about where the story's weight lies?
A text, a fallen wall and a foreign king's boast: each was made for a different purpose. What can each one tell you, and what can it not?
Is this line a complaint, an explanation, or a hint of what comes next? What in the book of Judges supports your reading?

l.t: Samuel, Saul and the Wish for a King
l.look: Samuel lists costs; the people name one benefit. Why might a community accept those costs? What does the passage suggest about how the text views the trade?
Why does Nathan tell a story instead of simply accusing the king? What can a parable do that a direct charge cannot?
Solomon says the building cannot hold God, then asks God to hear prayers made toward it. How do these two ideas fit together?
Count the years from the split to each fall. Why did the text's writers, living in Judah, have so much longer a story to tell about their own kingdom?
The passage says three times where the LORD was not. Why might a writer build a scene this way, and what does it prepare the reader to notice?

l.t: Assyria: One Kingdom Falls, One Survives
l.look: Each account was written by one side. Where do they agree, where do they differ, and what would you want to know before deciding what happened?
The verse does not say what the book was or where in the Temple it lay. What do the king's actions in chapter 23 suggest about what it said?
The text lists what was burned in order: Temple, palace, great houses. What does the order say about what the writer thought mattered most?
Which events in the book of Kings have outside witnesses, and which do not? What kinds of events tend to leave a mark in stone?

11.t: The Latter Prophets and the Writings
11.bq: What did the prophets and the Writings say to their first readers, and how do Jewish communities still hear them through the year?
std: Work out figurative and connotative meanings and the effect of repetition and sound in poetry.
Determine a source's central ideas and give an accurate summary free of prior opinions.
Teaching About Religion · expose not impose
Introduce a range of religious views without imposing any particular one.
11.write: Do the prophets and the Writings agree about how the world works? Choose two or three passages from this unit (for example Amos 5:24, Micah 6:8, Job 38:4 or Ecclesiastes 9:11) and explain what each says. Then show how two readers, such as Rashi, the Talmud, a modern scholar or a Christian reader, have understood one of them. End with what the passages together suggest and what they leave open.

ch.t: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the Twelve
ch.bq: What did the prophets say to their own people, and why are their words still read aloud every week?
ch.talk: Jeremiah and Hananiah both claimed to speak for God and said opposite things. How might a person in the crowd decide whom to believe?
ch.story: The Man in the Wooden Yoke

l.look: Which prophets spoke before Jerusalem fell in 586 BCE, and which spoke after? Why might that change what they said?
Compare this answer with Jeremiah 1:6, where the prophet says he is only a child and cannot speak. What do the two call stories have in common, and how do they differ?
For each pair, what connects the Torah reading and the haftarah? Is the link a shared story, a shared theme, or a contrast?
What is the same in the two translations, and what is different? How does one word change what a reader takes the verse to be about?
What happens first in the verse, and what happens after? Why might the order matter to the prophet?
The command is repeated twice and is addressed to a group, not one person. Whom might the prophet be telling to comfort the people, and why say it twice?
Which specific actions does Jeremiah list? Why might a crowd that loved the Temple be angry at this speech?

l.t: A New Covenant and a City in Mourning
l.look: The poet compares the city to a widow. What does that comparison say about what the city has lost, and about how the poet feels toward it?

l.t: Ezekiel: The Chariot and the Dry Bones
l.look: What clue inside the chapter supports the national reading? What in the language might lead a reader toward the resurrection reading? Can both be held at once?

Amos lived in a dry land where streams run only after rain. Why might he compare justice to a stream that never stops? Martin Luther King Jr. quoted this verse in 1963; what did he want it to mean for his listeners?
The verse lists three things. Put each in your own words. Which of them is about other people, and which is about God? Why might the prophet put them in this order?

l.t: Malachi and the Close of Prophecy
l.look: Obadiah has one chapter and Hosea has fourteen, yet all twelve count as one book. What might that tell you about how the scroll was put together?

ch.t: Ketuvim: Psalms, Wisdom, the Five Scrolls, Ezra–Nehemiah, Chronicles
ch.bq: What kinds of books make up the Writings, and why does the Tanakh end where it does?
ch.talk: Why might a community choose to read a book of love poems in spring and a book about loss in midsummer? What do the seasons add to the books?
ch.story: Five Scrolls, Five Holidays, One Year

l.look: Find the three parallel parts of this verse. What changes from one to the next: the verb, the group of people, or both? What is the effect of walking, then standing, then sitting?
Laments outnumber every other type. What might that say about when people most often turned to prayer in ancient Israel?
"Want" here means to lack. What does a shepherd do for sheep, and what is the psalm saying by using that picture? Why might this psalm be chosen for a house of mourning?
How can two opposite pieces of advice both be wise? What does putting them next to each other suggest about what a proverb is for?
Job says this before the poetry begins. Compare it with his demand in the poetry that God explain. Has Job changed his mind, or is he saying two true things at once?

The verses that follow list fourteen pairs of opposites. Is the poem saying that we choose the time, or that the time comes whether we choose or not? How does this fit the book's opening about breath?
Ruth lists four things she will share with Naomi. Which come first, and which last? Why might Jewish tradition read this speech as a model for joining the Jewish people?

l.t: Lamentations at Midsummer, Ecclesiastes in the Fall
l.look: The scrolls are listed here in calendar order, from Passover to Purim. Which holiday goes with each? Which scroll would take longest to chant?
Jewish commentators read "another place" as a hint of God in a book that never names God. What else could the phrase mean? Why might the author have left God unnamed?
What does each reader assume about what a prophecy is? Can a public school class describe both readings fairly without deciding which is right? How would you word it?
How many years passed between the decree and the finished Temple? Between the Temple and the walls? What might have slowed the work?

Compare this ending with the ending of the Torah (Deuteronomy 34) and of the Prophets (Malachi 3). What do all three endings have in common? Why might a collection end with an invitation rather than an arrival?

12.bq: What does a reader see in Genesis when the words are read slowly, with the text's oldest and newest readers side by side?
std: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence for what a text says outright and for inferences drawn from it.
Analyze how an author's choices about structure and order create effects such as tension or surprise.
Compare how two or more authors treat the same topic, including what each emphasizes.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
12.write: Does the narrator of Genesis judge the people in its stories, or leave judgment to the reader? Cite Genesis 25:34, Genesis 27:22 and Genesis 50:20, or another set of three passages from this unit. For each, say what the text states and what it withholds, and show how at least two readers (for example Rashi, Ramban, Genesis Rabbah, Alter or Auerbach) have handled it.

ch.t: Creation, Eden and the Akedah
ch.bq: What does a reader find in Genesis when the text is read slowly, word by word, with its oldest and newest readers at the table?
ch.talk: Why might a writer leave out what a character is feeling? What does the reader have to do when the text stays silent?
ch.story: Counting the Words Isaac Never Says

l.look: Ten words in English, seven in Hebrew. What does this verse say, and what does it leave unsaid about how, why, or when?
What changes about the story if verse one is a complete sentence, and what changes if it is only the opening clause? Which reading does Ramban need?
List one thing the two accounts share and two things Genesis does differently. What might each difference be saying?
Name two differences in order between the accounts. Then suggest one way Rashi might read them as one story and one way a modern scholar might read them as two.
Rashi says God asked so the man would not be afraid. What else could a question do that a statement could not? What does the man do with the opening he is given?

l.t: Eden in the Midrash and Beyond
l.look: Find one detail in Genesis 3 each reader might point to. How would you describe the difference between the two readings without saying which is right?
Genesis has 12 weekly portions and 50 chapters. Which of these divisions is older, the chapters or the portions? What would you need to know to answer?

l.t: Reading the Journey Word by Word
l.look: Count the steps before the name Isaac is spoken. Why might the text delay the name? What does Rashi do with the delay?
What would you have to add to the story to know how Isaac felt? Where does Rashi find a place to add something about Sarah?

l.t: The Ram, the Age and the Test
l.look: Each reader uses evidence. Name the evidence each one uses and the rule of reading behind it. Which kind of evidence do you find stronger, and why?

l.t: The Akedah in the Year and in Modern Thought
l.look: In this reading, who is the Akedah for, and what is the community asking for when the shofar sounds?

ch.t: Jacob, Joseph and the Art of Biblical Narrative
ch.bq: How does biblical narrative tell so much with so few words, and what do readers gain by reading the Jacob and Joseph stories as literature and as Torah?
ch.talk: The text never names the stranger. What does each reading, angel, Esau's angel, or Jacob's own conscience, do with the fact that Jacob walks away limping?
ch.story: The Man Who Limped at Sunrise

l.look: One parent's love is given a reason and the other's is not. What does the reader learn from the reason that is given, and from the reason that is missing?
The same Hebrew words open both moments. What has Judah done in chapter 37, and what happens to him in chapter 38? What does the repeated word ask the reader to conclude?
Name the parts that stay the same. Then say what each variation shows about the man at the well and about the woman he meets.
Isaac has evidence on both sides. What does he choose to trust, and what might the narrator be showing about how deception works?
Read the four reasons in order. What changes between the first name and the last? What does the reader learn about Leah that the narrator never says directly?
The name Jacob was explained at birth by his grip on Esau's heel. What does the new name say about him, and what does the limp add?
What evidence does each reader use? One reads the law; the other reads Jacob's words. Which parts of the chapter does each leave out?

l.t: Dreams, the Coat and the Pit
l.look: How many years pass between the pit and the palace? What do the paired sevens suggest about how the story is built?
List what Pharaoh adds. What do the additions tell you about the man telling the dream, and why might the narrator want the reader to compare?
Compare this with Judah's proposal in Genesis 37:26–27. What has changed in the man? What does he never mention, and why might that matter?
This is Joseph's reading of his own story. Does the narrator ever say the same thing? What is the difference between a character's interpretation and the narrator's?
Seven portions cover twenty-six chapters. Which portions break inside a chapter rather than at its start? What might that show about how the tradition divides the story?

13.t: Law, Covenant and the Prophetic Voice
13.bq: How do the Torah's covenant laws and the prophets' demands for justice belong to one conversation, and how have their readers carried it on?
std: Compare and contrast how several primary and secondary sources treat the same topic.
Analyze how specific word choices, including figurative language, build meaning and tone.
Analyze the relationship between historical sources and the interpretations built from them.
Teaching About Religion · aware not accepting
Build students' understanding of religions without pressing them to accept any one.
13.write: Amos, Hosea, Micah and Isaiah all say that worship without justice is unacceptable. Are they rejecting ritual, or demanding something of it? Argue from the text: cite Amos 5:21–24, Hosea 6:6 and one of Isaiah 1:11–17 or Isaiah 58:5–7, say what each passage says in its own context, and explain how at least two later readers (the Talmud, Avot de-Rabbi Natan, Ibn Ezra, Heschel, King) have read them.

ch.t: Sinai, the Decalogue and the Covenant Code
ch.bq: What does it mean that the Torah presents its laws as the terms of a covenant, and how have readers handled the hardest of those laws?
ch.talk: Both texts blame the owner who ignored a warning. Why might two societies agree about the owner but disagree about what happens to the ox?

l.look: Find the word "if" and the word "then." What does the sentence make depend on what?

l.t: The Shape of an Ancient Treaty
l.look: Which numbered parts can you find in the Exodus verses, and which parts are missing or found elsewhere in the Torah?
Which reading is closer to the plain sense (peshat)? What does each commentator gain by reading the way he does?
This sentence contains no "thou shalt." Why might Jewish tradition still count it as the first of the ten?

l.t: Three Ways to Count to Ten
l.look: Why does the Catholic count put this saying one place earlier than the other two? Which saying did it merge, and which did it split?
Which English word fits the Hebrew usage better? What might a reader gain, or lose, from each translation?
Hammurabi's laws are often called the first law code. What do these numbers say about that claim?
List every point where Exodus 21:28–32 agrees with this, then every point where it differs. Which list is longer?
The Talmud (Bava Kamma 84a) asks: what if a blind man puts out another's eye? How does that question push toward reading the verse as payment?

l.t: The Stranger, the Widow and the Orphan
l.look: The law gives a reason instead of a penalty. What kind of law works by reason rather than by threat, and why might the text choose that here?
Give one example from your own life where doing came before understanding. Does it help you see why Jewish tradition prized this order?

l.t: Shavuot and the Giving of the Torah
l.look: Which of these numbers come from the Torah's text and which from rabbinic calculation? Why does that matter?

ch.t: Amos, Hosea, Micah, Isaiah: Justice, Mercy and Return
ch.bq: What did the prophets demand of their hearers, and why do their words still open the prayer book and the protest march?
ch.talk: Amaziah calls Amos a troublemaker who should go home. Amos says he had no choice. Who is the audience meant to side with, and how does the text steer them?

l.look: What is Amaziah's argument, and what is Amos's? Which one talks about authority, and which about permission?
Water in a dry land comes and goes in seasonal streams. What does it mean to ask for justice that flows like a stream that never dries?
Why start with the neighbors? What would happen to the audience's attention if Amos had begun with Israel?

s.t: Hosea and Micah: Mercy and Requirement

l.look: What does it do to a message to make it a person's name, said every day at meals? Why might a prophet choose that method?
The first half says "and not"; the second says "rather than." Does the second half change how you read the first?
The verses before this list ever-larger offerings, ending with a firstborn child. How does that build-up change the force of the word "only"?
Five commands in one verse. Which are about courts, which about individuals, and who are the people named?
The first fast is something you do to yourself; the second is something you do for others. Why would the rabbis choose this to be read while the congregation is itself fasting?
All seven readings come from Isaiah 40 onward. What does that pattern suggest about how the rabbis heard the second half of the book?

s.t: Return: Teshuvah, Jonah and the Prophets Today

l.look: Maimonides makes the test of repentance a future event, not a feeling. Why might he set the bar there? Compare it with Hosea 14:2, which asks the nation to return.
Why does the book end with God's question and not with Jonah's reply? Whose answer is the book waiting for?
Five events in six years. What does the timeline suggest about how the prophets moved from the study to the street in that decade?

14.t: Poetry, Wisdom and the Scroll of Esther
14.bq: How do the poems and hard books of the Writings let readers argue with suffering, time and power, and why did Jewish tradition keep them?
std: Determine a theme and analyze in detail how specific details develop and shape it.
Analyze how specific word choices, including figurative language, build meaning and tone.
Compare how two or more authors treat the same topic, including what each emphasizes.
Teaching About Religion · study not practice
Teach about religious practices without having students take part in them.
14.write: Does the Tanakh think the world is fair? Argue from Job 42:7, Ecclesiastes 3:9 or 9:7, and Esther 4:14. Say what each passage says and how at least two readers (the friends, the Talmud, Maimonides, Rashi, a modern scholar) have read it.

ch.t: Psalms and the Song of Songs: Hebrew Poetry
ch.bq: How does Hebrew poetry work, and why have Jewish readers heard a love song as the holiest book of all?
ch.talk: Rabbi Akiva called a book that never names God the holiest book in the Writings. What might a reader have to believe about reading in order to say that?

l.look: Match each word in the first half with its partner in the second half. Where does the second half go further than the first?
Label each verse synonymous, antithetic or synthetic, and say what the second (or third) line adds. Which verse resists the labels?
Each of these poems is built on the 22-letter alphabet. Which number is a multiple of 22, and what does that tell you about the poem's plan? Psalm 145 has only 21: what might have happened?
Before this verse the psalm speaks about God as "He." Here it speaks to God as "Thou." Why might the poet make that change exactly at the darkest point?
The verse names a place, an action and a memory. Which of the three does the rest of the psalm keep returning to, and what does the poem say happens to a person who forgets it?
Mark the address, the complaint, the plea and the turn. What is missing between the plea and the turn, and how would you fill the silence if you were reading the psalm aloud?
The verse pairs love with death and jealousy with the grave. Is this synonymous, antithetic or synthetic parallelism? Why compare love to death at all?
What in the verse allows both readings? What would each reader say the other is missing?
Which of these sets is tied to the week, which to the festival year, and which to every single day? What does the pattern suggest about how the Psalms are used?
Write four line pairs about a place you know, using one governing image. Then write a fifth pair that turns. Read it aloud and mark where the second line of each pair goes beyond the first.

ch.t: Job, Ecclesiastes and Esther: Questions Without Easy Answers
ch.bq: What do a book about undeserved suffering, a book that calls everything breath, and a book that never names God have in common?
ch.talk: Why might a tradition keep a book in its Scripture that never mentions God? What does the noise at Haman's name add to the reading that silence could not?

l.t: A Story in Prose, a Poem in the Middle
l.look: This is the Job of the prose frame. Compare it with the Job of chapter 3, who curses the day he was born. Are these the same man? What might the author be doing by giving us both?
Job asked why he suffers. God asks where Job was at creation. Is this an answer, a refusal to answer, or a change of subject? Defend your reading with what the friends said earlier.
What is at stake in whether Job was real? Would the book teach the same thing as a parable? Why might the Talmud leave the question open?
Read the verse three times, once with each word. How does the book's mood change? Which translation best fits a speaker who also says to enjoy your bread with a merry heart?
List the fourteen pairs from 3:2-8 in two columns, harsh and gentle. Does the order suggest that the gentle side wins, the harsh side wins, or neither? What does verse 9 do to your answer?
The sages kept a book because of its first and last lines. Reread 12:13. What does it let a reader do with everything in between? Is that a fair way to read a book?
Mordecai never says God. The rabbis read "another place" as a hint. What does the verse say will happen with or without Esther, and what does that imply about who is in charge of the story?

l.t: Purim: Laughter With a Commandment Inside
l.look: Feasts drive the plot of Esther from the first chapter to the last. Why might a book about a hidden God be built around parties? What do the four duties of Purim borrow from the story?
What question is each reader asking? Do their readings conflict, or can a single reader hold all three? What is lost if the chapter is skipped?
Answer the student's question using at least one verse from each book, cited by chapter and verse. Then say which book's answer you find most convincing and why the other two were kept anyway.

15.bq: How did the words of the Tanakh reach us, and what does it mean to read them in translation?
std: Analyze change and continuity within and across historical eras.
Analyze the relationship between historical sources and the interpretations built from them.
Determine the meaning of words in a text, including how an author develops a key term.
Integrate information from diverse sources into a coherent understanding, noting where they disagree.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
15.write: Choose one verse from this unit (Genesis 1:1–2, Isaiah 7:14, Deuteronomy 32:8, Micah 6:8 or Psalm 19:8). Set out what the Hebrew says, what two witnesses or translations (such as the Masoretic Text and the Septuagint, or JPS 1917 and the King James) do with it, and how Jewish and other readers have read the result. Then argue: what must a reader of English know to read this verse fairly?
rooms: How to read a sacred text — the room

ch.t: From Scroll to Codex: Masoretes, Scrolls and Versions
ch.bq: How did the words of the Tanakh travel across two thousand years of copying, and how do we know what the oldest copies said?
ch.talk: If you found a book a thousand years older than any other copy, what would you compare first, and what would count as a big difference?
ch.story: A Stone, a Jar and a Cave

l.look: Which one book of the Tanakh is missing from the caves, and why might a single missing book not tell us much?
This verse reads the same in the Great Isaiah Scroll and in the medieval Hebrew text. What kind of claim does the verse make, and why might a copyist have taken it as encouragement?
Which explanation would you find more convincing, and what evidence would settle it? Why might a prayer book keep the received text even so?
What does the story want its readers to believe about the translation? Which details do that work?
The 24 and the 39 contain the same text. How can the same words be counted as 24 books and as 39? What does the Catholic count add?
A rule of textual study says the harder reading is often older, because copyists smooth, not roughen. Apply that rule here. Then say why it might not settle the question.

In Hebrew this verse is seven words written with consonants only. The Masoretes added the vowels a reader had always supplied. Why might a community want that pronunciation written down, and what could be lost by fixing it?
Why would a tradition count words and letters rather than just reading carefully? What kind of mistake would a letter count catch that a word count would miss?
How many years separate the Isaiah scroll from the Aleppo Codex? Why is a complete codex from 1008 more useful to an editor than a damaged one from 930 that scholars consider more accurate?
Use the rules from the lesson. Which reading best explains how the other two arose? Then say what Rashi's reading of the received text adds that textual criticism does not ask about.

l.t: Bomberg's Bible and the Text Today
l.look: Each edition is made for a different reader with a different question. Name the reader and the question for each. What would each reader miss if handed one of the other two?

ch.t: Translating the Tanakh
ch.bq: If every translation is an interpretation, what does a reader gain and lose in moving from Hebrew to English, and who decides?
ch.talk: Should a translation use one English word for one Hebrew word every time, or choose the best fit each time? What does each choice cost the reader?

l.look: Find the words that differ. Which version sounds like a story continuing (Now the earth was) and which like a fresh statement? What does each opening make you expect next?
List every difference between the two, including the small ones (the, a, capital letters). Which differences are grammar, and which carry a tradition of reading?
Match each reader to one of these: King James, JPS 1917, NJPS 1985, Alter, Fox. Give a reason for each match. Is there a reader for whom two versions would be better than one?
How many years passed between the two JPS translations? What had changed in American Jewish life and in biblical scholarship that might explain why a new one was wanted?
Which translator would you want for a first reading? Which for a close study of the story's repeated phrases? Can a footnote solve the problem, or does it just move it?
What does a reader gain from Yitzhak, and what does a reader lose? Should a translation for a public-school class use one, the other, or both?
Replace chesed in turn with mercy, kindness and loyal love. How does the verse's demand change with each? Which English word would you choose, and what would you write in a footnote?

JPS 1917 and the King James write living soul; several later translations write living being. What does each English choice suggest about what a person is? Which fits Genesis 1, where animals are also called nefesh?

Which English word fits a poem that compares the thing praised to honey? What does each translation assume about what the psalmist loves? Where else in the course have you met torah as law, and where as teaching?
The name is tied to a verb, not a noun. What might it mean for a name to be a form of to be? Why might a tradition decide that such a name is not to be spoken?
Do the exercise with what this chapter has taught you. Then answer: is any one of the three Bibles the right one for a public-school classroom, or does the lesson depend on having all three?

16.bq: How has one text been read so differently across a thousand years, and how can we describe those readings fairly without deciding which is true?
std: Analyze the factors and context that shaped people's perspectives in different eras.
Evaluate authors' differing points of view on the same issue by weighing their claims, reasoning and evidence.
Evaluate an author's premises, claims and evidence by corroborating or challenging them with other sources.
Teaching About Religion · educate not promote or denigrate
Present every tradition fairly, neither advancing nor disparaging religion.
16.write: Choose Isaiah 53:4, Genesis 1:26 or Genesis 1:1. State what the verse says in JPS 1917. Then present two readers from this unit (for example Rashi and Ramban, Rashi and Augustine, or Genesis Rabbah and a historian) and explain what question each asks and how each answers it from the text. Cite the verse and the reader by name. Close by saying what a fair description of both readings must include.

ch.t: Midrash, Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Maimonides
ch.bq: How did Jewish readers across a thousand years turn one text into a conversation, and what was each of them asking?
ch.talk: Why might a tradition choose to print its disagreements on the same page as its sacred text, instead of settling them and printing only the winner?

l.look: What feature of the text does this midrash start from, and what would you need to know to decide whether it is explaining the verse or replacing it?
Which two verses does the midrash link, and what does the parable of the architect add that the verses alone do not say?
In Deuteronomy the verse says the commandment is near and doable. How does Rabbi Joshua in Bava Metzia 59b give the same words a new job, and is that use a peshat reading or a midrashic one?
Rashi reads the first word as "in the beginning of God's creating," a heading for what follows. What changes about the verse if it is a heading rather than a statement of the very first event?
Ibn Ezra says this verse holds a secret and that the one who understands will be silent. What in the word "then" might have caught his eye, and why might he have chosen not to explain?
What does it mean to disagree with someone "with hidden love"? What would a commentary look like if it hid the rebuke and showed only the love?

l.t: Radak and the Book of Roots
l.look: Which of these readers could have met? Who was only answering the written words of a person long dead?

l.t: Maimonides and the Torah's Words for God
l.look: Maimonides opens the Guide by arguing that "image" here cannot mean a physical shape. What problem does he think a literal reading causes, and what does the verse mean on his reading?

l.t: The Zohar and the Four Levels
l.look: How does the garment image treat the plain sense of a story: as false, as unimportant, or as something else? Compare it with Rashi's aim of giving the plain sense.
How many years passed between Rashi's death and the first printing of his commentary? What does that gap tell you about how the commentary survived?
Sort the four readings into peshat, remez, derash and sod. Then pick two and explain what question each reader was trying to answer, and why the answers do not cancel each other.

ch.t: Jewish, Christian and Academic Readings of the Same Text
ch.bq: When a rabbi, a pastor and a historian open the same chapter, what is each of them asking, and how can we describe their readings without ranking them?
ch.talk: The professor says the three readers are not asking the same question. What is each one's question, and how would you know if one of them had answered it well?

l.look: The Tanakh and the Protestant Old Testament have the same content. Why are the numbers 24 and 39, and what does the Catholic count add?
Compare this ending with Malachi's promise of Elijah. What mood does each leave a reader in, and what does each invite the reader to do next?

Read the verse once as a sign given to King Ahaz about the next few years and once as Matthew 1:23 reads it. What does each reader have to assume about the word almah and about the timing of the sign?
Who is "we" in this verse? Try the verse with "we" as the nations speaking about Israel, as Rashi reads it, and with "we" as Christians speaking about Jesus. What changes, and what stays the same?

l.t: Psalm 22: A Cry in Two Traditions
l.look: Describe how a Christian reader on Good Friday and a Jewish reader on Purim would each hear this verse. Then say what a textual scholar would want to check before deciding which reading is older.
For each of the three readings, name the evidence the reader brings from outside the verse. Which readings could all be held at once by one person, and which could not?
Is Ramban's distinction between law and story a fair rule of reading or a convenient escape? What would you need to know about how Jews used aggadah before 1263 to decide?
Which of these events were ordered by a ruler and which were voluntary? What changed between the second row and the third?
How does this method differ from Rashi's, which begins with the text but also with the tradition's readings? What can each method see that the other cannot?
Which of these works asks who wrote the text, which asks how the text works as literature, and which asks what the ground shows? Group them.
List three things the stele shows and three things it cannot show. Then say how a maximalist and a minimalist might each use the same stone.
Take one of the three well scenes. Write the question each of the four readers would bring to it, and one thing each might notice that the others would not.

17.t: The Tanakh in Jewish Life and Capstone
17.bq: How does a text keep living in the practices, arguments and speech of the people who read it, and how do you join that conversation honestly?
std: Cite strong textual evidence, linking details to an understanding of the text as a whole.
Write arguments with precise claims, fairly developed counterclaims and well-chosen evidence.
Draw evidence from informational texts to support analysis, reflection and research.
Teaching About Religion · study not practice
Teach about religious practices without having students take part in them.
17.write: Choose one verse this unit read closely (Genesis 22:2, Deuteronomy 26:5, Genesis 4:8 or Deuteronomy 6:8-9). Quote it in JPS 1917. What does the text do with its words, and how have two readers read it? Cite the verse, one commentator on it (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Ramban or a midrash by collection and section) and one practice or modern reader from the unit, and state one reading that differs from yours.
rooms: World Religions capstone — the sources speak

ch.t: The Tanakh in Prayer, Holiday, Home and Literature
ch.bq: How does a book written more than two thousand years ago keep living in prayer, in the calendar, on a doorpost and in the words of a city?
ch.talk: What is the difference between reading a text in a classroom and touching it on a doorframe every day? What can each kind of reading notice that the other might miss?

s.t: The Prayer Book as a Mosaic

l.look: The verse is addressed to "Israel" and then speaks of "our God." Who is speaking to whom here, and why might a community choose a verse that is a command to listen as the center of its prayers?
About what share of the book of Psalms is recited in these fixed sets alone? Why might a community choose to repeat a small number of psalms rather than read the whole book in order?

l.t: The Song of the Sea Each Day
l.look: Find the two halves of the verse. How does the second half complete the first? Why might a community choose to repeat a battle song every single morning, and what does the midrash about the angels add to that choice?
Add the rows. Genesis is the longest book and Leviticus the shortest, yet the counts are close. What does that suggest about how the portions were divided, by length or by story?

l.t: The Haggadah and a Wandering Aramean
l.look: Which reading makes a better opening for a story about rescue from danger? Which fits a farmer thanking God for land? What does each reader gain and give up?
All five books are short. Why might short books be chosen for public reading on a holiday? Which pairing seems to match by season, and which by theme?
The verse says "them" without saying which words. What do the mezuzah and tefillin decide "them" means? What would a reader like Rashbam, who saw a figure of speech, say the verse is asking?
List what the verse states and what the practice adds. Who made the additions, according to tradition? What does this example show about how a short verse becomes a living custom?

s.t: The Text in the Wider World

l.look: How does knowing the Ezekiel verse change the way the anthem's line sounds? What is the poet doing when he echoes a verse and reverses it?

l.t: Go Down, Moses: The Text in American Voices
l.look: In Leviticus 25 the verse is about the jubilee year, when land returned to its families and Israelite bondservants went free. What did the bell's makers take from the verse, and what did they leave behind? Is that a fair way to use a text?
How many years passed between the city's founding and its first congregation? Between the Parliament and the Supreme Court decision that frames this course? What changed in each gap?

ch.t: Capstone: Arguing an Interpretation from Text and Commentary
ch.bq: How do you build an honest argument about what a passage of the Tanakh does and how its readers have read it?
ch.talk: Dev and Rosa never decided who was right. What did they produce instead, and why might that be worth more in a class about how a text has been read?
ch.story: One Verse, Four Voices, Two Chairs

l.look: Which questions does the text itself raise, and which do the students bring to it? Which could two careful readers answer differently by pointing at lines? Rewrite the weak ones.
Read the verse aloud, then read it with "Isaac" moved to right after "son." What changes in how the command lands? Which order does the King James Version use, and why might a translator smooth it?
What does the repetition do to the reader's sense of Abraham? Why might the middle answer add "my son"? Write one sentence of peshat, with no commentary, about what the pattern shows.

Mark the exact spot where something is missing. Then compare two fillings: the Septuagint's "Let us go into the field" and Genesis Rabbah's quarrel over dividing the world. What does each filling assume about why the text is silent?
What question about the verse is Rashi answering? What does his reading assume about how the Torah uses words? Could a peshat reader explain the four descriptions without a dialogue?

l.t: Ibn Ezra and Ramban Answer Back
l.look: Which reader is arguing from what the text says, which from what it does not say, and which changes the question? Which move would you use in your own capstone, and why?

l.t: A Modern Reader at the Table
l.look: The midrash and the modern reader notice the same gap. How do their responses differ? What question could you ask about Sarah that stays with the text and does not become a verdict on the tradition?

l.t: A Thesis About What the Text Does
l.look: Which thesis can be disagreed with and checked against lines? Which one asserts something about God rather than about the text? Rewrite A and B so they make claims about what the text does.
How many centuries separate the midrash from Rashi, and Rashi from Alter? What does that span suggest about the phrase "a conversation across time"?

In Deuteronomy the verse says the commandment is near and doable. How does Rabbi Joshua reuse it in the Talmud's story? Is that a peshat reading or a derash reading, and does that matter for the point he makes?
What does the image of iron on iron say about how a good study partner treats you? What kind of question sharpens, and what kind only cuts?
Which three criteria carry most of the weight, and why do you think the course put it there? Where would a beautifully written paper with no citations lose the most?
